Chapter 2. Key Concepts

Source: vignettes/articles/02-Key-Concepts.Rmd
02-Key-Concepts.Rmd

This chapter introduces the ideas the rest of the guide relies on. There is no code here.

2.1 Ambient RNA

During tissue dissociation some cells break open and release their RNA into the cell suspension. When the suspension is loaded onto a droplet device, this free RNA is captured in every droplet together with the intact cell. After sequencing, each cell’s counts are a mixture:

observed counts = the cell’s own RNA + ambient RNA

Ambient RNA is dominated by the most abundant and most fragile cell types. In a brain sample, for example, neuronal transcripts can appear in microglia; in a blood sample, haemoglobin and immunoglobulin genes appear in every cell.

2.2 The soup

The soup (or ambient profile) is the composition of the ambient RNA: for every gene, the fraction of ambient molecules that belong to that gene. It is the same for every droplet in a sample, because all droplets draw from the same suspension.

2.3 Empty droplets

Most droplets in a run contain no cell. They still capture ambient RNA, so their counts are a direct measurement of the soup. A typical 10x run has hundreds of thousands of empty droplets with between 1 and 100 UMIs each. Decant adds them up to estimate the soup.

2.4 The contamination fraction (rho)

The contamination fraction, written rho (ρ), is the share of a cell’s counts that are ambient. A rho of 0.05 means 5% of the cell’s UMIs came from the soup. Typical values are 0.02 to 0.10 for single-cell data and higher, up to 0.30, for single-nucleus data. Rho differs from cell to cell: smaller cells and nuclei carry relatively more ambient RNA.

2.5 How Decant estimates rho

Some genes are not expressed by a given cell type at all. Haemoglobin, for example, is not made by T cells. Every haemoglobin count in a T cell must therefore be ambient. Decant finds, for each cluster, the genes that the cluster does not express (the absent genes) and asks how much soup would be needed to explain the counts it sees for them. That amount is rho. The cluster estimate is then refined for each cell.

This is why Decant needs clusters: it looks for absent genes cluster by cluster. Clusters from your usual Seurat analysis work well.

2.6 How Decant removes contamination

Once rho and the soup are known, the expected ambient count of every gene in every cell is rho × cell total × soup fraction. Decant removes that expectation, gene by gene, with two guarantees:

  • a corrected count is never negative, and
  • a corrected count is never larger than the observed count.

Decant offers four rules for distributing the removal; the default, bayes_cell, is explained in Chapter 7.

2.7 Ambient RNA and differential expression

In a case/control study, samples can carry different amounts of soup. If diseased tissue is more fragile, its samples contain more ambient RNA, and that RNA is rich in the disease genes of the abundant cell types. A standard test on a rare cell type then reports those genes as changed in the rare type. Decant’s ambient_de() puts each sample’s measured soup into the statistical model, so the test separates real expression changes from changes in the soup (Chapter 9).

2.8 Glossary

Term Meaning
Ambient RNA, soup Cell-free RNA captured in every droplet
Soup profile Fraction of ambient molecules per gene
Empty droplet A droplet without a cell; it measures the soup
rho (ρ) Fraction of a cell’s counts that are ambient
Absent gene A gene a cluster does not express; its counts in that cluster are ambient
UMI Unique molecular identifier; one UMI is one captured molecule
Pseudobulk Counts of one cell type summed per sample
Gate An automated test against a known answer that a component must pass
